card.profile_long: Wotagei (ヲタ芸), also known as otagei (オタ芸), is a dance and cheering style performed by wota, fans of Japanese idol singers, especially those of Hello! Project, AKB48, and Vocaloid idols like Hatsune Miku. It involves jumping, clapping, arm-waving, and chanting slogans, often with glow sticks or penlights, creating light trails known as cyalume dance. The practice developed from the ōendan cheering squads of the 1970s and 1980s, where fans shouted calls in unison and coordinated movements to support idols. The term wotagei is a contraction of "the art of idol otaku" (アイドルオタクの芸), distinguishing it from general otaku culture. Wotagei performances include named techniques such as thundersnake, rosario, amaterasu, and muramasa, combined choreographically to fit songs. The MIX call pattern, originating around 1993, is used during intros and instrumental breaks. The 2002 single "Romantic Ukare Mode" by Miki Fujimoto is closely associated with wotagei, featuring a sequence of signature moves. A notable event occurred in 2004 when 100 to 200 fans performed wotagei to this song outside Saitama Super Arena, and the footage spread widely. Wotagei expanded beyond concert halls to anime conventions and fan gatherings, aided by video sharing platforms like YouTube and Niconico Douga. In the 2010s, wotagei evolved into a professional performance art, supported by groups like GinyuforcE, who popularized cyalume dance worldwide and appeared on Japanese TV. The Cyalume Dance World Battle, started in 2018, formalized competitive wotagei performance. Styles include cyalume-gei, using glow sticks, and chikagei, focusing on full-body movement. Wotagei techniques are tied to song sections, with chorus moves like thundersnake and romance forming the core choreography. The dance is closely linked to Japanese idol fan culture and remains a vibrant, evolving tradition practiced internationally.

sections.origins_and_history: Wotagei originated from the ōendan cheering squads of the 1970s and 1980s, where fans shouted calls and coordinated movements to support idols. The practice of MIX calls began around 1993 at idol venues. The 2002 single "Romantic Ukare Mode" by Miki Fujimoto became emblematic of wotagei, and in 2004, 100 to 200 fans performed it outside Saitama Super Arena, spreading the dance widely. Wotagei gained mainstream attention around 2006 with video sharing platforms. It expanded beyond concerts to anime conventions and fan gatherings. In the 2010s, it developed into a professional performance art with groups like GinyuforcE pioneering cyalume dance. The Cyalume Dance World Battle began in 2018, formalizing competition. Wotagei remains active globally, with ongoing performances and events.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Wotagei is performed by wota fans, often holding glow sticks or penlights, called uchishi. It involves jumping, clapping, arm-waving, chanting slogans, and complex choreographed sequences of named techniques such as thundersnake, rosario, amaterasu, muramasa, romance, OAD (over action dolphin), and PPPH (clap-call rhythm). The dance is structured around song sections: MIX calls during intros and instrumentals; OAD and ni-hai-o-hai during verses; rosario and PPPH in pre-chorus; and chorus techniques like thundersnake and romance. Movements include swinging the body side to side, crossing arms, sliding on the ground (sliding romeo), and rhythmic clapping. Beginners start by learning basic chorus techniques like thundersnake, muramasa, and romance. The tempo matches the song, and performances require space, often done at the back of venues or outside. Technique is highly coordinated but varies by style (cyalume-gei with glow sticks or chikagei with full-body movement).
sections.music_and_instruments: Wotagei is performed to Japanese idol music, especially songs by Hello! Project, AKB48, and Vocaloid idols. The music features structured sections (intro, verse, pre-chorus, chorus) that guide the choreography. The rhythm is typically upbeat J-pop with clear beats for calls and claps. Glow sticks (cyalume) or penlights are essential instruments for visual effect. Vocal chants and calls are integral, with patterns like MIX and PPPH. The mood is energetic and supportive, matching the idol concert atmosphere.
sections.costume_and_setting: Performers are fans (wota) usually dressed casually or in fan-related attire. Glow sticks or penlights are standard accessories. Wotagei is performed at idol concerts, anime and manga conventions, fan meetings, and sometimes outside venues or at DJ events. Because of space needs, performances often occur at the back of venues or designated areas at festivals. The setting is informal but energetic, with a communal atmosphere.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Wotagei is performed to support Japanese female idol singers during concerts and public appearances. It also occurs at anime conventions, fan gatherings, and special events like birthday celebrations of idols. It expresses fan enthusiasm, unity, and artistic support. The dance has evolved into a performance art and competitive discipline, with events like the Cyalume Dance World Battle. It is a cultural expression of idol fandom and community identity.
sections.notable_figures: Miki Fujimoto is notable for her song 'Romantic Ukare Mode,' closely associated with wotagei. The group GinyuforcE pioneered cyalume dance and popularized wotagei worldwide, appearing on TV and releasing instructional DVDs. Kita no Uchishitachi and Fly-N are prominent wotagei teams with large online followings. Zero-uchi Restart is a recent group with significant social media presence and commercial releases. The Wotagei Association organizes national competitions.
sections.regional_variants: Wotagei is practiced mainly in Japan but has spread internationally, including Taiwan and North America. Styles include cyalume-gei (using glow sticks) and chikagei (full-body movement). Some techniques are associated with specific communities or venues, such as yellow panchos at DearStage or raion blade at Okinawan idol shows.
sections.lineage: Wotagei descends from 1970s ōendan cheering squads supporting idols, evolving through idol fan culture and the development of choreographed cheering and light-stick dance. It shares roots with Japanese organized cheering traditions but is distinct in its integration with idol music and fan identity.

claims.text: Wotagei is a type of dancing and cheering gestures performed by wota, fans of Japanese idol singers, involving jumping, clapping, arm-waving and chanting slogans.
Wotagei originated with shin'eitai cheering groups for idols around the 1970s and 1980s, whose members shouted calls in unison in time with the music.
The practice of MIX, the specific pattern of calls during intros and instrumental breaks, started at idol venues around 1993.
Miki Fujimoto's 2002 single Romantic Ukare Mode became the song most associated with wotagei.
On May 2, 2004, an estimated 100 to 200 people performed wotagei to the song at Keyaki Hiroba outside Saitama Super Arena, and this footage became widespread.
Wotagei performances using glow sticks and penlights are also known as cyalume dance.
GinyuforcE were pioneers of cyalume dance and helped spread wotagei worldwide through YouTube.
The first Cyalume Dance World Battle was held in 2018 with finals at Kanda Myōjin Hall.
